    "body": "Archive Extraction Category: Action Execution | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Extracting an archive means executing a promise made by untrusted bytes: a manifest of names, sizes, and attributes that the extractor must not believe. This skill covers detecting the real format, bounding the total decompressed size, rejecting traversal paths, and extracting into a staging area so nothing extracted is used before validation completes. When to Use Use when ingesting bundles, backups, datasets, or dependency archives into a working environment. Do not extract untrusted archives into privileged paths, and do not treat extension names as format evidence. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The archive file on disk | | | | Yes | Staging directory for extraction | | | | No | Decompression-bomb ceiling (default 1 GiB) | Procedure 1. Detect the format from magic bytes (PK\\x03\\x04, ustar, gzip, xz), never from the file extension. 2. Read the entry manifest; reject the archive if declared total size exceeds the ceiling. 3. Validate every entry name: reject absolute paths, segments, and non-materializable entries such as device nodes. 4. Verify checksums when the archive provides them (CRC, or sidecar signature files). 5. Extract into the staging directory with permissions normalized; do not execute or import anything during extraction. 6. Move validated files into the destination only after every entry passed. Outputs | Output | Type | Desc ription | |---|---|---| | | | Validated paths now in the destination | | | | Rejected entries with reasons | | | | Format, counts, sizes, checksum results | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Zip bomb | Compressed ratio and total size unchecked | Enforce on declared sizes | | Path traversal | Entry names contain or absolute paths | Validate every entry name before writing | | Extension spoofing | A gzip stream named fed to the wrong parser | Detect format from magic bytes | | Partial success | Extraction stopped mid-archive but reported done | Extract to staging; report skipped entries | | Overwritten files | Destination already contained same-named files | Stage first, then move with explicit overwrite policy | Security and Authority Boundary Archives are untrusted input with code-execution risk: entries can be executable or symlinks pointing outside the staging tree. Extract with least privilege, never auto-run extracted code, and treat any archive from an unknown source as hostile until validated. For each step, define its compensating action — the reverse operation, an acknowledge-and-correct path, or explicit not-compensable. 3. Define failure handling as a saga: on failure at a given step, run compensations for all earlier steps in reverse order. 4. Record semantic invariants — what the compensations must restore in meaning, not just me chanics — and check them after recovery. 5. Plan for compensation failure: retry the compensation, then fall back to a recorded manual-intervention path. 6.     "body": "Idempotent Retries Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A retry that re-applies a side effect is worse than the original failure: duplicate charges, double sends, repeated writes. This skill makes an operation idempotent before retrying it — the caller attaches a stable operation key, the receiver dedupes, and the effect happens once regardless of how many attempts the network takes. When to Use Use for any operation with side effects that might be retried — payments, emails, writes, external state changes — especially across network boundaries where timeouts make outcomes ambiguous. Generate the operation key once per logical operation, before the first attempt, and reuse it on every retry. 2. Design the receiver to dedupe on the key: return the original result for a repeated key instead of re-applying the effect. 3. Check current state before applying the effect — the operation may already have succeeded on a previous attempt. 4. Retry only on retryable failures — timeouts and transient errors — with exponential backoff and a stated attempt cap. 5. Treat ambiguous outcomes, such as a timeout after send, as pending rather th an failed: resolve by querying the receiver with the key before retrying. 6. Record the operation key in the audit trail so duplicates are explainable after the fact.
